Percentage of nodes in the biggest connected subgraph. Low values mean your data is fragmented — entities that should be related aren't linked yet.

Total number of nodes (entities) in the current graph.

ja/securityPage.json::securityPage.purpo: Scope a rule to a single table, or to a whole domain so it covers every table in it; where both apply, the table rule wins for that table. A rule is written against a role rather than a person, so what someone can see is changed by changing the role they hold.

ja/securityPage.json::securityPage.roleP: A role also carries its own ceilings: requests per second, and limits on query depth, node count, and execution time. That is how a role can be given reach without being given unbounded cost — an expensive query is refused by the role that issued it, not by the source it would have hit.

A role is the unit every other permission is written against. Its capabilities decide which operations it may run, and its domain access decides which parts of the model it can reach at all. Row-level rules, and the access checks on every surface, name a role rather than a person — so what someone can see and do is changed by changing the role they hold.

ja/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.bit: Append-only bitemporal history. off = ordinary materialization (each refresh replaces the data; no history). snapshot = each refresh appends the whole fresh dataset stamped with its system time; simplest and works on any engine, but storage grows by full size per refresh. delta = each refresh appends only the rows the engine computes as changed, plus tombstones for removed keys; smaller, and needs an entity key. Comma-separated column(s) identifying the ENTITY being tracked (e.g. customer_id) — the identity each new version belongs to. If this MV keeps multiple states of the same entity — over time, or along any other dimension — that entity appears on many rows, so the entity key is NOT unique in the table and therefore is NOT the primary key — the row's PK is a surrogate (or entity + system-time). Used to reconstruct state 'as of' a time: partition by this key and take the latest version at that time. Required for delta mode (no key means no delta); in snapshot mode it groups versions for as-of reconstruction.

ja/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.cha: How Provisa learns rows changed. ttl = refresh on the Cache TTL timer; probe = source-native freshness query, re-pull only on change; ttl_probe = probe after the TTL floor elapses; native/debezium/kafka = source push. ja/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.con: per-instance — each instance its own copy

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. It decides whether the materialized view is ONE copy shared by all instances, or a separate copy per instance. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot — pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy independently — simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so only safe for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Where the copy lives depends on the federation engine's store: per-instance only makes sense when each instance has its OWN store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a SHARED external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared — per-instance has nowhere private to write and would just clobber.

Its options depend on Time Travel (keep history): OFF stores current state only — replace (overwrite everything) or upsert (merge by primary key); ON keeps history — snapshot (append the whole fresh result as a new version each refresh) or delta (append only the rows that changed, plus tombstones for deletes). Optional preflight check run after the view SQL and before landing: define preflight(streams, ctx) and return a VERDICT — ctx.ok() to continue, ctx.abort(reason) to reject (error + poison downstream), or ctx.quarantine(reason) to hold without landing. streams is a dict keyed by input node: streams["schema.table"] yields that input's rows lazily, so you inspect an input without materializing it. A check inspects; it does NOT transform rows (put transforms in SQL or an external processor). A SQL-expressible check — if any(...)/all(...) over one input's rows — is pushed down to the engine as a count probe over that input, so it scales to a billion rows; anything else streams each input as Arrow batches and short-circuits. Call ctx.warn(reason) for a non-fatal advisory. It MUST be deterministic — no clock, randomness, imports, or IO — and is purity-checked when you save; a non-deterministic or unsafe check is rejected.

ja/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.upd: Keeps history (time travel), compactly. Every refresh appends ONLY the rows that changed (plus tombstones for deletes) as new versions — you can still query 'as of' any time, but storage grows only by the change, not the whole result. The classic way to maintain a full change history / audit trail of a source without storing a full copy each refresh. Needs an entity key to identify the entity across versions.

The query is NOT re-run. The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key — so work per refresh scales with the SIZE OF THE CHANGE, not the whole dataset. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It applies only when all three hold: (1) exactly ONE input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta — i.e. it runs on a change/CDC signal, not full snapshots, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column) so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. Also needs a primary key. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), it falls back to a full recompute for that refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct. Work per refresh scales with the TOTAL size of the inputs, not with how much actually changed.

Keeps history (time travel). Every refresh appends the ENTIRE fresh result as a new version stamped with its time — you can query the table 'as of' any past refresh. Simplest history model and works on any engine, but storage grows by the full result size every refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key: matching rows are updated in place, new rows inserted, nothing deleted-and-reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size — only the write is by key.

ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step0.descripti:
🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. Leave whenever — click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is a governed query compiler for federated data that stays out of the data path.

🎯 The whole core is one short exercise: connect some databases, then query them seven ways — or skip the syntax and just ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop: no servers, no infrastructure to stand up (that comes later, when you're ready).

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCPPostgres · pgwireNeo4j · BoltJDBC · Java/JVMArrow Flight SQL · ADBCDuckDB · airport

Everything after that — more sources, federation, files, relationships, views, scheduled pipelines — is how you grow with the platform, not what you need on day one. We'll flag where the core ends.

Ready? Let's connect a source. →

ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step1.descripti:
Everything you want to federate is registered here:
🗄️ Databases🏢 Warehouses🔌 APIs📄 Files☁️ SaaS

🤖 The seventh surface lets an agent reason with your data. It drives the very same governed tools — search the catalog, describe tables, run SQL, follow relationships — and chains them to answer questions no single query could, every call bound by your role's governance.

🔌 The same MCP server plugs into Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or any MCP client, so agents explore and reason over your model the governed way.

One surface left — the one that writes all seven for you. →

ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step14.descript:
✅ You just saw it end to end: one source, queried seven ways — or just asked in plain English. That's the whole promise — and you could stop right here.

Press Esc anytime; 🧭 the compass up top replays this tour whenever you want.

👉 Everything ahead is how Provisa grows with you — optional depth, not required steps:

  • 🔗 Link tables across sources into one graph
  • 🔐 Govern it — roles, row-level security, column masking
  • 🏗️ Build a delivery pipeline — views, a materialized warehouse, lineage
  • ⚙️ Operate it — pick an engine, ship to production

Keep going? →
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step14.title: That's the five-minute core
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.descript:
Relationships link tables across sources — even across different databases — turning flat tables into a traversable graph.

🛡️ They can also be enforced: hand people freedom to explore, with sensible guardrails.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.title: Connect the graph
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step16.descript:
🔗 Map a source column to a target column and set cardinality:
1 → 11 → ∞∞ → ∞

✨ Or let Provisa infer relationships for you with AI.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step16.title: Define a relationship
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step17.descript: The entity-relationship diagram renders your whole federated model — every registered table and the relationships between them.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step17.title: See the ERD
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step18.descript:
🔐 Registering a table sets per-column access, wired straight into roles:
👁️ Read✏️ Write

That's role-based access control — and the roles themselves are defined here on the Security page.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step18.title: Access control (RBAC)
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step19.descript:
🔎 Once roles exist, go finer — restrict which rows each role sees with attribute-based predicates:

region = user.region AND status != 'archived'

📐 Data-driven and enforced per row — across every source and protocol.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step19.title: Row-level security
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.descripti: ➕ New connections start with this button — PostgreSQL, Snowflake, MongoDB, a REST API, a CSV, and 30+ more.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.title: Register a source
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descript:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here — no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views — over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands — governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data — invokable from every surface, fully governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts — declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics — governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once; every surface — SQL, GraphQL, AI agents — computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descript:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars — recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar, not just a clock.
  • 🗄️ Store As… — replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel — bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descript:
🧬 Lineage isn't opaque. This is a real query, analyzed. Each result column is traced back through its transforms — follow name_upper — and joins to the exact source columns that feed it.

Commands are declaratively defined, so every step is captured; materialized views retain full lineage by definition. Nothing runs — the query is only analyzed.

→ Last stop: operating it in production.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descript:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine — pluggable: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime — the model, the surfaces, and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach — Parquet, Iceberg, Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials auto-provisioned. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability — redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step — no rewrite:

  • Develop — embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale — Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote — point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.title: Operate it
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step24.descript:
🎉 You're back where you started. Now make it yours:
  • 1️⃣ Register one of your real sources
  • 2️⃣ Expose a few tables, draw a relationship or two
  • 3️⃣ Query it from Explore in any language:
SQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIREST

Point pgwire or Bolt tools at it — everything just works.

📚 The Docs tab has the full guides. 🧭 The compass up top replays this tour anytime. Enjoy Provisa.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step24.title: That's the tour — now make it yours
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.descripti:
One connector list spans every category:
  • Databases — PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Greenplum
  • Cloud warehouses — Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse
  • Analytics / OLAP — ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot
  • Lakes & files — Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hive, Parquet, CSV, JSON
  • NoSQL & graph — MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis, Neo4j
  • APIs — REST, GraphQL, gRPC
  • Streaming — Kafka
  • Enterprise SaaS — SharePoint, Splunk · plus government data subscriptions
Pick one, fill the connection, Save. The list isn't fixed — the native federation engines are extensible: declare a custom Postgres FDW or DuckDB extension in config and Provisa reaches a new source type, no code.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.title: 53 source types
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.descripti:
Whatever the source — a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint, a graph — Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.title: Everything becomes a table
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.descripti:
Choose a source, schema, and table, then pick columns — each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking — redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility — show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases — rename for the model

That's the whole setup — a source and a few tables. 🚀 Now let's query it. →
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.title: Pick columns & policy
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.descripti:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source — join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. And the model's own metadata and every activity trace are themselves queryable tables here — join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 Not just this explorer — the same governed SQL runs through multiple wire protocols; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire — every Postgres-compatible client — psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI — connects out of the box.
  • JDBC — drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline, or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL — columnar streaming for ADBC clients — no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport — ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.title: SQL (1 of 7 surfaces)
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.descripti:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

Grouping and aggregates over your relationships — 🎯 one endpoint, 📖 self-documenting schema.

🔌 Hit it from any GraphQL client — Apollo, Relay, urql — and, with federation enabled, drop Provisa into an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 7 surfaces)
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.descripti:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources — no single graph database required.

🔌 And any Bolt client — Neo4j Browser, Bloom — runs that same traversal over the wire, no code change.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.title: Cypher (3 of 7 surfaces)
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.descripti:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Call it from any gRPC client — 📐 strongly typed, 🚀 high-throughput.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 7 surfaces)
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary.de: 📖 Every term links back to the columns that carry it — curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps: ✨ Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and ✨ Relationships proposes links across the whole glossary. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPreview.des: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview — live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityPane: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column — null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness — and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityTabl: 🧪 A data-quality checker — Soda or Great Expectations — registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.
A quality checker is just a source
ja/tour.json::tour.steps.stepReports.des: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports — usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health — each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.
